lore: The old chapel by the well has its doors open again, and a big, broken-nosed man named Prior Hale is sweeping the steps. He teaches the holy spells to anyone with the calling: smite what needs smiting, and when the fight turns, pray. Brother Ansel has been seen there every morning since.
plain: A new class: the priest. Casts holy spells from a pool of mana and can (P)ray mid-fight to heal. Learns spells at Prior Hale's Cha(p)el. Choose it when you make a new character.

lore: Mother Quill has been telling anyone who'll listen that a mage's power comes from the mind, not the arm. The town clerk, tired of arguing, has updated the register: warriors are measured by their Strength, thieves by their Dexterity, and mages by their Intelligence.
plain: Each class now names its main attribute: Strength for warriors, Dexterity for thieves, Intelligence for mages. Same numbers as before.

lore: Mother Quill would like it known that a mage who has learned Frost Needle does not go about throwing Fireballs. Every spell has its greater form, and now you'll know its name: Frost Nova, Thunderclap, Blizzard, and on up.
plain: A mage's special is now named for the spell they know (Frost Needle unleashes Frost Nova, Firebolt unleashes Fireball). Same power and mana cost as before; press (U) to unleash it.

lore: Somebody finally pointed out that a mage hitting a goblin with a dagger is embarrassing for everyone. A door you hadn't noticed off the square now has a lamp in the window: the library, where Mother Quill keeps the spells and decides who's fit to learn them. Mages wake each morning with a well of mana, and spend it as they like.
plain: Mages now cast spells and use mana: (C)ast your spell, (F)ireball for more mana, or S(t)aff to save it. Mana refills each day. Learn stronger spells at Mother Quill's (L)ibrary as you level, instead of buying weapons.

lore: The roads you know are still free to walk, but they aren't empty. The farther you go, the likelier you are to meet someone, or something, along the way.
plain: Traveling to a place you've already explored is still free, but long trips can now turn up an event on the road.

lore: Not everything you pick up in the wild is just loot. Some things belong to someone, and some people in town are waiting for a favor. Keep your ears open and your bag closed. The shop will always buy, but it rarely pays best.
plain: Side quests: some events, conversations and finds start a quest that plays out over a few days. Check your journal under (G)ear.

lore: The town clerk, who has never once been in the forest, has decided it's misleading to count your day in forest fights when most of it is spent walking. From now on it's simply turns: a hunt is a turn, a step into the wild is a turn.
plain: "Forest" on the status line is now "Turns". Nothing else changed: hunting and each step into the wild still use one.

lore: The wild isn't only teeth and claws anymore. Out past the gate you might find a traveler bleeding by a rock, a shrine with coins gone green in the bowl, a troll under a bridge with a riddle and a grudge, or a ring of mushrooms humming in the grass. What you do about it is up to you. What comes of it isn't.
plain: Exploring now turns up events besides fights, a few a day: pick a choice, and see what happens (gold, healing, charm, gems, an extra fight, places marked on your map, or trouble).

lore: The town has learned to write. Leave a letter for Hilde, or Violet, or Odile at her bench, and sooner or later a reply turns up in your mailbag, in their own hand. Sir Pomfrey's arrive sealed in wax.
plain: Townsfolk and characters now answer your mail, usually within an hour or two. One reply a day from each, covering everything you sent them.

lore: People in this town talk, if you let them. Stop and pass the time with whoever's about. Odile at her bench, Violet behind the bar, Pip in the square. You never know what someone will let slip. And if the Cartographer is in town, she might take a pencil to your map.
plain: You can talk to townsfolk and characters who are around (just ask the narrator to talk to them). The Cartographer, when she visits, may mark nearby places on your map.

lore: A new sign hangs off the square: ODILE, GEMCUTTER, burned into the wood. She has a loupe screwed into one eye and opinions about your ore. She'll sell you a pickaxe, and the caves in the hills, cold and dripping and three levels deep, will give a little to anyone who swings one. Not too much a day. Things live down there too.
plain: Caves are open: (D)escend at a cave mouth, then (M)ine with a pickaxe (6 swings a day, apart from forest fights) or go (D)eeper. Take ore and gems to Odile's (W)orkshop in town to have jewelry made: one piece worn, adding strength, defense or charm.

lore: The townsfolk have started wanting things. Hilde talks about a cottage by the river, Brother Ansel passes a hat for the shrine, and Pip won't stop saying he'll outrank someone. Don't be surprised to meet one of them out past the gate, or to find one gone for the day. And if you rob one, expect to be remembered.
plain: Townsfolk now have goals and choose what to do each day, so they're less predictable. You may meet them in the wild, see their goals in the news, and a townsperson you rob may come after you.

lore: The town gate stands open, and beyond it the land goes on: old woods, wet fens, hills that climb toward broken crags. Nobody has mapped most of it. The first to find a place gets talked about in the tavern; the farther you go, the worse the things that live there.
plain: (E)xplore replaces the Forest. Walk the world one step at a time (each step into the wild costs a forest fight, going home is free), hunt where you stand, and check your (M)ap. Somewhere in the hills there are caves.

lore: A small correction from the town clerk: the healer's apprentice is Rowan, and always was. Anyone may court anyone in this realm, and the clerk would like that noted in the register.
plain: The healer's apprentice is Rowan (he/him); Jory uses they/them. Anyone can court and marry anyone.

lore: Hearts in this town have grown harder to win, and easier to lose. A wedding now takes real luck, and the locals have started courting too. Sir Pomfrey, in particular, has bought a new cloak.
plain: Weddings are rarer (charm helps a little, not a lot), and townsfolk can now marry, so they can win your spouse away.

lore: Violet has competition. The healer has taken on an apprentice with ink on his fingers, the lamplighter walks the square after dark, and a juggler comes through at the weekends. And charm, at last, buys you something: shopkeepers knock a little off, and bards seem to sing a bit more kindly.
plain: Court Rowan (healer, by day), Mara (square, at night) or Jory (square, weekends), each with their own marriage perk. Charm now gives shop discounts and better luck with bards and visitors.

lore: Violet remembers now. A wedding is a wedding: she won't marry you twice, she'll keep a room aside for you at half the price, and if someone else catches her eye, the whole town will hear about it before you do.
plain: Marriages to Violet last, she can only be married to one player at a time (so she can be won away), and her spouse gets rooms at half price.

lore: The square has people in it now. You'll catch the locals coming and going at their usual hours, other adventurers loitering by the well, and most days someone from out of town with a cart, a story, or a rumor they're dying to share.
plain: The town square shows who's about right now and a visitor of the day. Talk t(o) them once a day for a rumor and, sometimes, a small gift.

lore: The town has had a word with its more inventive citizens. The healer won't patch you up mid-swing anymore, a room at the inn only protects you while you're actually in it, masters now send you off bruised instead of dead, and the dragon, it turns out, comes back.
plain: Fairness fixes: no healing, shopping or banking mid-fight; leaving your room to fight ends its protection; losing to your master isn't fatal; the dragon returns at the daily reset; new characters can post, mail and attack from level 2.

lore: The town has been tidied. The square is where the roads meet; the tavern keeps its own company, with rooms upstairs; the forest keeps you until you choose to walk out. You go in, you do your business, you come back out.
plain: Each place has its own short menu. (R)eturn to town to go somewhere else. The Inn is now upstairs in the (T)avern.

lore: Every so often now, a blow lands exactly right: through the gap in the armor, square between the eyes. It doesn't happen often. For mages it happens a good deal more, which the forest's larger residents are beginning to notice.
plain: Critical hits: any swing can land for double damage. Warriors and thieves crit 3% of the time, mages 17%. Works in player fights too.

lore: Thieves have always had quick hands. Lately they've had quicker feet: a Sneak Attack now often lands before the beast can answer, and the forest seems to drop its valuables in a thief's path a little more often than anyone else's.
plain: Thieves: Sneak Attack dodges the counterattack half the time, and thieves find loot more often (5% vs 3%).

lore: The town crier has been asked, politely, to stop following you into your place of work. He took it well. The news will keep until you come through the gate.
plain: No more realm news or mail notes at the start of your Claude Code sessions. Nothing shows until you enter; the ⚔ and ✉ in the status line still do.

lore: There's music in the tavern now, and not always the same music. Some nights it's a cheerful piper, some nights an old man with a ballad that never ends, a minstrel singing about himself, or a woman in the corner who barely speaks. Ask nicely. A good song can do strange things for you.
plain: A bard plays the (T)avern each day — Fennick Reed, Dunstan the Unfinished, Corwin Lark or Wren. (L)isten once a day for a song and, sometimes, a small gift.

lore: You step outside and the sky looks familiar. It ought to: it's the same one over your own roof, more or less. When it rains where you are, it rains in the forest too.
plain: The realm's weather follows your real weather, from your rough location (never stored). Ask to turn it off any time.

lore: There are new faces in town. A monk is up before the roosters, the stable lad has found a sword, a fortune teller has hung a curtain in the back of the tavern, and someone called Sir Pomfrey would like you to notice his armor.
plain: Four new townsfolk: Brother Ansel, Pip, Madam Orsolya and Sir Pomfrey. They show up in (R)ankings and the tavern.

lore: There's a new page nailed to the inside of your door, in a hand you don't recognize. It seems to know what's changed in the realm since you last slept, and it means to tell you.
plain: After an update, the game tells you what's new, once.

lore: Your name is cut a little deeper into the inn's sign now, with a small mark beneath it. When the realm shifts, you'll feel it before anyone tells you.
plain: The title screen shows your version, and the game tells you when an update is out.

lore: A crossed pair of swords has been scratched into the corner of your vision. It glints whenever something happens in the realm that you haven't heard about yet.
plain: ⚔ N in your Claude Code status line for news you haven't read. (N)ews clears it.

lore: The old sign over the gate has come down in the night. The new one is carved in heavier wood: Dragon's Door.
plain: Dragonmoor is now Dragon's Door. The command is /dragons-door:enter.

lore: Someone has painted the dragon over the gate, wings and all. You'll see it each time you come through.
plain: A title screen when you enter.

lore: A small envelope seems to hang at the edge of your sight whenever a letter is waiting, even when you're busy with other work.
plain: ✉ N in your Claude Code status line. Set it up with /dragons-door:statusline.

lore: A pigeon loft has gone up behind the inn. Letters come and go now, and the townsfolk keep their own hours — some at dawn, some long after dark.
plain: (M)ail to send and read letters. Townsfolk play at different times through the day.

lore: You wake and notice something new in your room. A brown leather satchel sits in the corner, its strap worn soft. Now and then, a beast in the forest drops something worth keeping.
plain: Rare loot drops, and a bag to carry them in. (G)ear to look inside; bigger bags at the shop. Die, and you lose one thing from it.
